entries.title: TikTok agrees to settle with Alabama state over teen safety
entries.summary: The settlement involves TikTok adding several child safety measures to its platform including time limits and increased parental control. It is similar to a recent settlement competitor Meta had reached.
entries.content:
September 26, 2026

The settlement involves TikTok adding several child safety measures to its platform including time limits and increased parental control. It is similar to a recent settlement competitor Meta had reached.

Short-form content sharing platform TikTok and its Chinese parent company ByteDance reached a settlement with Alabama, the southeastern US state said on Friday, days ahead of what would have been a revealing trial over teen safety and its impact on their mental health.

As part of the deal, TikTok agreed to pay $100 million (€87.7 million) to the state of Alabama and enact measures for teens including a two-hour daily use limit, restricted access for children and pauses after 15 minutes of use.

However, the payout could rise to $300 million if 40 other states sign similar agreements with the company within a stipulated time period, the document said.

What have TikTok and Alabama state said after the settlement?

"This builds on our commitment and core objective to continually ​enhance our robust safety tools to protect teens," a spokesperson for TikTok's US operations said in a statement.

Alabama Attorney General Steve Marshall sued the social media giant last year.

At least 27 other states and Washington DC have brought similar lawsuits. Apart from these, TikTok faces thousands of lawsuits by individuals, school districts and municipalities over its impact on teen mental health. Meta Platforms, Snap Inc and Alphabet's YouTube are also defendants in many of these ​cases.

"This is a great day for Alabama parents. Tonight, they can rest easier knowing real protections are in place to shield their children from the dangers of social media addiction. TikTok has agreed to give parents real control over what their kids see and how much time they spend on the app," Marshall said in a press release.

With this, the company has settled all cases selected for trial against it, including claims by five young people and a Kentucky school district.

What were the allegations against TikTok?

The state of Alabama had argued that TikTok's endless stream of videos makes it the most addictive of social media platforms and that its algorithm specifically pushes young users toward content about violence and self harm.

The state held the app partially responsible for a teen mental health crisis and a significant increase in emergency room visits.

The lawsuit also accused TikTok of falsely claiming that it limits access to sexual and violent content for young users to have the app rated as 'safe for teens' on app stores.

It said that TikTok asks users to self-report their ages but also allows them to evade questions by viewing videos without creating an account.

That still earns the company data on viewing habits. Being able to scroll videos without signing in makes 'Kids Mode' an entirely useless feature, the lawsuit said.

What measures will TikTok take?

As per the settlement, TikTok has to implement a series of safety measures, including:

  • Two-hour daily limit
  • Additional parental control limiting time on platform
  • 'Productive pauses' interrupting continuous scrolling after 15 minutes, 60 minutes and 90 minutes
  • Restrict children access from 12 a.m. to 6 a.m.
  • Restrictions on push notifications during night and school hours
  • Robust measures to verify user age
  • Limits on discoverability of teen accounts by adults
  • Sending parents notifications of suspicious interactions between teen users and adults
  • Blanket ban on use of cosmetic filters by teens
  • Non-personalized feed for teens

Last month, Meta agreed to pay a massive $17 billion to 47 US states and territories in a similar case while agreeing to make changes to teens' access to its platforms, Facebook and Instagram.

It did not admit wrongdoing and conditioned $5 billion of the payout on TikTok, Snap and YouTube's adoption of the same terms. TikTok has not commented publicly about that deal.

Edited by: Rana Taha

entries.title: Yemeni leader calls for general mobilization against Houthis
entries.summary: Amid military escalation with the Iran-backed Houthis, the Saudi-backed head of Yemen's governing body urged his compatriots to join the government forces.
entries.content:
Yemen

Yemeni leader calls for general mobilization against Houthis

September 25, 2026

Amid military escalation with the Iran-backed Houthis, the Saudi-backed head of Yemen's governing body urged his compatriots to join the government forces.

Rashad al-Alimi, the head of Yemen's Saudi-backed Presidential Leadership Council, on Friday called for a general mobilization in the war-torn country.

"I call upon the sons of our great people to engage in general mobilization and national mobilization, to rally around their armed and security forces," al-Alimi, who is also Supreme Commander of the Yemeni Armed Forces, said in a televised address.

The head of the governing body urged his compatriots to join the government forces weeks after Yemen's government was dealt a major blow by the Iran-backed Houthi rebels.

The Houthis have seized control of Yemen's entire Red Sea coast in a lightning offensive, allowing them to fully control the strategic Bab al-Mandab Strait, igniting global fears about shipping through the chokepoint.

What else did Yemen's leader say?

In his address, al-Alimi also said that the objective of the mobilization is to "restore state institutions and extend sovereignty over the entire national territory," including the Yemeni capital of Sanaa, which has been under Houthi control since 2014.

He added that anyone who defects from the Houthis to the government will be pardoned in an upcoming amnesty.

Al-Alimi addressed residents of Houthi-controlled areas, urging them to protect their children and not send them to fight alongside the Houthis.

"The state does not view you as a party to the conflict but as its people and partners," he said.

Houthis escalate conflict

For more than a decade, the Houthis have been fighting Yemen's Saudi-backed government. Although a 2022 truce left the conflict largely frozen, fighting has recently flared up again amid the wider conflict involving Iran.

In recent weeks, the Houthis have intensified their missile and drone attacks on neighboring Saudi Arabia. They declared a maritime blockade and attacked Saudi targets in an attempt to stifle Saudi oil exports.

The Houthis accuse the kingdom of besieging Yemeni areas under their control. They attacked Riyadh for the first time in years over the weekend, marking a major escalation.

Edited by: Rana Taha

entries.title: Lula or Bolsonaro as president? Brazil gears up to vote
entries.summary: Brazilians go to the polls on October 4. The front-runners are multilateralist incumbent Lula da Silva and former President Jair Bolsonaro's son, Flavio, who wants to bring Brazil closer to the US and away from China.
entries.content:
Brazil

Lula or Bolsonaro as president? Brazil gears up to vote

September 25, 2026

Brazilians go to the polls on October 4. The front-runners are multilateralist incumbent Lula da Silva and former President Jair Bolsonaro's son, Flavio, who wants to bring Brazil closer to the US and away from China.

Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva spoke in no uncertain terms at the opening of the UN General Assembly on Tuesday in New York: "Brazil does not belong in anyone's backyard," the Brazilian president said. His comment was directed at his US counterpart Donald Trump, despite Trump not being in attendance.

The US president has repeatedly interfered with Brazilian domestic politics, siding with former President Jair Messias Bolsonaro and the far-right opposition. In July, Trump imposed sanctions on a judge who found Bolsonaro guilty of attempting a coup and sentenced him to 27 years in jail. Washington only lifted the sanctions after negotiating with Lula.

Bolsonaro's eldest son Flavio is Lula's biggest challenger in the upcoming presidential election on October 4, and polls currently show the two of them to be neck and neck in a potential runoff.

The election in the world's fifth largest country is drawing a great deal of international attention. Brazil is an agricultural giant and very rich in natural resources — boasting rare earth elements, vast water resources and enormous crude oil reserves.

Brazil one of South America's last bastions of the left

Lula is the "last man standing" of the South American left, while Flavio Bolsonaro is part of an increasingly strong far-right camp. Argentina, Bolivia, Peru, Chile, Ecuador and Colombia all have governments that are sympathetic to Trump. And since January, Venezuela has been what some describe as a US protectorate.

Foreign policy hasn't played a big role in the campaign, but this election will nonetheless decide whether Brazil moves closer to Trump's US. Washington is seeking economic and military dominance in South America through the Shield of the Americas initiative, focused on combating violent cartels. After his military intervention in Venezuela, Trump is now exerting economic pressure on Mexico and Cuba. At the same time, he is trying to counter Chinese influence in the region.

For his part, Lula is an advocate of multilateralist diplomacy, wanting Brazil to engage in dialogue and trade with everybody. China has long been Brazil's most important trading partner.

Flavio Bolsonaro favors a conservative alliance with the US and other right-wing states. But for Leonardo Paz from the Brazilian Fundacao Getulio Vargas think tank, a Bolsonaro victory would not necessarily automatically mean better relations with the US. He told DW that Lula had established a largely normal relationship with Trump — both are 80 years old — despite some initial friction. The two leaders got along well, said Paz, even if Lula has not succumbed to Trump's pressure.

Paz did admit that if Bolsonaro won, the 45-year-old would be more likely to accommodate Trump, pointing out that his father Jair had made far-reaching concessions to the US when he was president. During Jair Bolsonaro's time in office from 2019 to 2023, Brazil agreed to forgo its "developing country status" in World Trade Organization negotiations in exchange for a mere promise that the US would back its bid to become a member of the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD). Trump also said he was considering giving Brazil NATO "privileges." Neither promise came to anything.

"While relations with the US would continue as they are with Lula, it is completely unclear what a Flavio Bolsonaro presidency would mean," Rubens Ricupero, a former Brazilian diplomat and minister, told DW. "Lula has prestige in foreign policy, while Bolsonaro is completely inexperienced."

Would Brazil pull out of BRICS?

A victory for Bolsonaro would likely jeopardize Brazil's role in BRICS, the alliance that comprises Brazil, Russia, India, China, South Africa and five other states. Bolsonaro has said that one of his first acts would be to review whether Brazil should stay in the alliance, arguing that BRICS only serves to provoke the US. He has also spoken out against China's efforts to reduce the global dominance of the US dollar.

It's hard to tell how serious such intentions are, considering the importance of economic ties between China and Brazil. Javier Milei, Argentina's current president, also engaged in harsh rhetoric against China before he came to power, but quickly adopted a more conciliatory tone once in office to not jeopardize Chinese loans.

"Political relations with China would likely cool, but I wouldn't expect any substantial changes in economic and commercial relations," predicted Ricupero in case of a Bolsonaro victory.

Paz agreed that Flavio Bolsonaro was unlikely to take an extremely aggressive stance toward China in case of victory. He explained that, like Milei, Jair Bolsonaro had engaged in some sharp rhetoric against Beijing at the beginning of his term but had quickly softened his tone, given the fact that Brazil's agricultural sector in particular is so dependent on China.

Paz pointed out that the Bolsonaro family enjoyed most support in Brazil's rural regions, which made good money with China. "The unknown factor with Flavio Bolsonaro is how much pressure the US would exert so that Brazil distanced itself from China and to what extent he would yield to the pressure," said Paz.

Brazil not likely to become major world player

Paz said that despite possessing enormous natural resources that are important to the global economy, Brazil would likely remain a minor player on the world stage as it had neither the economic strength to provide financial aid to other countries nor the military strength to help resolve conflicts. "This severely limits Brazil's ability to act," he said.

But Brazil could continue to be a major protagonist in the Global South, he said, as it is under Lula. "This is particularly evident in the international debate on global governance, in which Brazil raises issues such as new trading conditions, climate policy and development," he said.

Ricupero said Lula carried particular weight in foreign policy, especially regarding the environment and climate change. "His commitment to addressing ecological challenges was clear from his choice of [leading environmentalist] Marina Silva as environment minister," he said.

The former diplomat said he feared Flavio Bolsonaro would repeat the mistakes of his father, and this was one of the reasons the election was drawing such attention from around the world. He pointed out that Brazil had become more isolated after Jair Bolsonaro dismantled major environmental policies, adding that relations with the European Union had particularly suffered and negotiations on a trade agreement between Mercosur and the bloc had been put on hold. The deal was finally signed early this year.

This article was originally written in German.

entries.title: Germany news: Parliament approves fuel tax cut
entries.summary: German lawmakers hope to drive down fuel prices by cutting taxes on gas and diesel from October 1. Meanwhile, Germany's defense minister visited Budapest to ramp up defense and military ties.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany news: Parliament approves fuel tax cut

Published September 25, 2026last updated September 25, 2026

German lawmakers hope to drive down fuel prices by cutting taxes on gas and diesel from October 1. Meanwhile, Germany's defense minister visited Budapest to ramp up defense and military ties.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • A fuel tax cut passes Bundestag as Germany faces high gas prices
  • A state minister reportedly pushes plan to limit asylum right
  • Germany's Defense Minister Pistorius in Budapest

  • Left Party approves launch of exploratory coalition talks with Greens, SPD after Berlin election

  • Students across Germany go on strike against potential return of military conscription

This blog, on Germany's biggest headlines on Friday Sept 25, 2026, has now closed. 

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.

Skip next section German FM Wadephul visits Canada as it prepares to become EU associate member

German FM Wadephul visits Canada as it prepares to become EU associate member

German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul took a one-day break from the UN General Assembly in New York to visit Canada.

In light of the discussion about Canada’s possible associate membership in the European Union, he has called for people not to focus on words.

“In my view, this is less about terminology and more about ensuring that we truly deepen our cooperation in key areas,” Wadephul said during a meeting with his Canadian counterpart, Anita Anand, in the capital, Ottawa.

Wadephul said that both Canada and the EU have shown "great interest" in further deepening cooperation. The German government welcomes this and will hold further discussions on the matter, he added.

Wadephul and Anand signed a confidentiality agreement to facilitate the exchange of classified documents. This agreement was expected to bring significant benefits, particularly with regard to enhanced military and defense cooperation.

Skip next section Berlin: Left Party approves launch of exploratory coalition talks with Greens, SPD

Berlin: Left Party approves launch of exploratory coalition talks with Greens, SPD

The socialist Left Party, which triumphed in last week's state election in Berlin, is set to initiate exploratory discussions with the Greens and Social Democrats (SPD) on forming a new government in the German capital.

On Friday evening, delegates at a party conference approved the move by a large majority. The leadership of the far-left party is expected to formally invite both parties to begin talks potentially as early as next week.

The Greens have already agreed to the talks. Berlin SPD leader Steffen Krach has also expressed a willingness to participate. However, he emphasized that these talks would not automatically lead to formal coalition negotiations.

In Sunday's election, the Left Party received 25.7% of the vote. The conservative Christian Democrats (CDU) followed with 18.8%, the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) with 16.3%, the Greens with 14.3%, and the SPD with 12.1%.

Based on the results, only three-party alliances have enough seats for a majority. A CDU-SPD coalition is currently governing Berlin.

Skip next section BASF chemicals giant seeks to take over Evonik

BASF chemicals giant seeks to take over Evonik

German specialty chemicals company Evonik on Friday confirmed prior media reports that rival BASF is seeking to take over the company based in Essen. 

BASF, an industrial giant listed on the main DAX stock market, has approached Evonik about a possible voluntary takeover offer for all of the company's shares, Evonik said. It said that at present talks were not taking place.

The confirmation follows reports in the specialist press, first from trade publication Dealreporter and then from the Financial Times.

Evonik is listed on the MDAX, the stock market for the 50 companies ranked immediately below the 40 largest companies on the primary DAX index.

Predominantly owned by the RAF Foundation, Evonik is the second-largest chemicals company in Germany — after BASF — and one of the largest specialty chemicals companies in the world.

Should BASF's acquisition bid succeed, it would require approval from German and EU competition authorities.

The Ruhr-based company is also a longstanding and prominent sponsor of football club Borussia Dortmund.

Skip next section Bundesliga-winning former Hamburg captain Peter Nogly dies aged 79

Bundesliga-winning former Hamburg captain Peter Nogly dies aged 79

One of the most beloved and decorated players in the history of Hamburger SV, defender and captain Peter Nogly, has died aged 79.

Nogly captained Hamburg during their glory days in the late 1970s, winning the Bundesliga, the German Cup and the European Cup Winners' Cup.

Hamburg said on Friday that he had died after a long illness, hailing "an outstanding personality and guiding figure" as well as "an absolute fan favorite and one of the best defenders in club history."

Nogly played 320 Bundelisga matches for Hamburg and captained the club in 122 games, a record only surpassed by fellow club legend Uwe Seeler. 

Nogly, known for his imposing stature, was nicknamed Eiche, "the oak." But the sturdy giant was also fair, never once being sent off in his lengthy career in Hamburg's defense.

Despite his integral role at one of the best clubs in Germany, he never really broke into the national team setup, only representing what was then West Germany four times at the senior level.

Nogly left Hamburg to play in North America, before returning to Germany to conclude his career. He held several lower league coaching and managerial roles after retirement.

Skip next section Pistorius visits Budapest, plans 'restart' of military cooperation with Magyar government

Pistorius visits Budapest, plans 'restart' of military cooperation with Magyar government

German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius is in Hungary, announcing plans to reboot military cooperation with the EU and NATO member in light of this year's change of government. 

"Berlin and Budapest are growing politically closer together again," Pistorius said alongside his counterpart Romulusz Ruszin-Szendi in Budapest.

"This is a restart of relations between our countries, and that in turn is excellent new for our countries, for our people, but also for the entire NATO alliance and the European Union," he said.

Hungary's previous government under former Prime Minister Viktor Orban was perceived as unusually friendly towards Russia, certainly by NATO and EU standards, and critical of its neighbor Ukraine. 

New Prime Minister Peter Magyar has campaigned on seeking a reset to ties with Brussels, Kyiv and NATO. 

Defense Minister Ruszin-Szendi said, "We will be allies again. We will act as is expected of us and as we expect of our allies."

During his visit, Pistorius also went to Europe's largest synagogue, the Dohany Street Synagogue or Great Synagogue in Budapest.

Skip next section New law will make e-scooter companies liable for accidents, rather than renters

New law will make e-scooter companies liable for accidents, rather than renters

Companies renting out e-scoooters to the public will in future be liable for accidents involving the vehicles. 

A new law to this end passed the Bundesrat upper house of parliament on Friday. 

The idea is to make it easier for victims or people negatively affected by e-scooter crashes to claim compensation.

At present, the people renting the scooters are liable for accidents. Quite often these are minors, who should be covered by their parents' or guardian's general liability insurance — something all German residents are obliged to procure.

While any user of the rented scooter should therefore be covered, in practice it can often be prohibitively difficult or time-consuming to track them down and coordinate a claim.

The law will also apply to grey areas where it can be even more difficult to identify a responsible E-scooter user. For instance, as well as crashes, it would cover cases such as a pedestrian tripping and falling because of an E-scooter being parked or deposited in an illegal or dangerous place.

Until now, would-be claimants would have needed to demonstrate who had parked the scooter, which could be difficult or even impossible if companies allowed anonymized hiring and usage.

E-scooters are treated like bicycles, with less stringent insurance requirements than those for motorized vehicles which require bespoke personal insurance for legal road usage.

Skip next section READ: Volkswagen, Audi to recall almost 1 million cars in Germany

READ: Volkswagen, Audi to recall almost 1 million cars in Germany

Germany car making giant Volkswagen and its subidiary company Audi  are to recall nearly a million vehicles in Germany due to steering problems, according to media reports.

Skip next section Germany's Heidenau bans new Stolpersteine dedicated to victims of Holocaust

Germany's Heidenau bans new Stolpersteine dedicated to victims of Holocaust

The town of Heidenau, near Dresden, has banned new Stolpersteine (stumbling stones) on the public streets, with the center-right CDU and the far-right AfD voting together to curb the installation of new memorial plaques bearing the names of Holocaust victims.

The city's administration urged against the motion. The initiators, however, argued that placing the plaques in the street leads to "passersby walking over or even stepping onto the names of the victims."  They suggested honoring Holocaust victims at one of the city's cemeteries instead.

With the local branch of Friedrich Merz's CDU joining forces with the AfD to pass the motion, it has also raised questions about the political "firewall" against the far right pledged by mainstream German parties.

The International Auschwitz Committee described the CDU support as scandalous.

"This is a transparent and despicable attempt to drive Nazi victims in Heidenau out of the city once again and dispose of them where, according to the AfD, their memory has belonged a long time ago — at the cemetery," said the organization's Executive Vice President Christoph Heubner.

Skip next section Bundestag passes fuel tax rebate

Bundestag passes fuel tax rebate

Lawmakers in the Bundestag, Germany's lower house of parliament, approved a temporary cut to the fuel tax on Friday.

The government will ​cut ‌taxes on gas and diesel by about €0.17 per liter startig from October to the start of the new year in an effrot to help ​citizens cope with prices that have jumped since the Iran war.

It's the second time this year Germany has temporarily cut the fuel tax. The measure is expected to cost the federal and state governments €2.5 billion in lost tax revenue.

Skip next section Berlin can afford housing expropriations, German researchers say

Berlin can afford housing expropriations, German researchers say

Germany's socialist Left Party, which won the most votes at the recent Berlin election, is planning to tackle the city's housing crisis by expropriating large companies that own 3,000 or more apartments in the German capital. The plan has already triggered strong opposition from the federal level, including center-right Chancellor Friedrich Merz, who has pledged there would be "no expropriation of private property in Germany."

A new study by economic researchers, including scholars from Germany's independent Macroeconomic Policy Institute (IMK), found that the Left's plan can be funded without breaking the bank.

The researchers found that Berlin can afford to expropriate around 210,000 apartments while paying some €13.5 billion in compensation to the corporate owners. The study, published on Friday, indicates such a move could be done without slowing down the construction of new homes or new budget cuts in the city-state.

The paper warns that expropriation would not solve the housing issues without widespread construction of new homes, but it adds that the move could be an additional element in tackling the affordability crisis.

Skip next section Condor airline: UK investor Attestor to buy out German state share

Condor airline: UK investor Attestor to buy out German state share

Condor, one of Germany's biggest airlines, will be fully owned by UK investor Attestor by the end of August next year.

The German federal government and the Hesse state government currently own nearly half of the company. The state authorities acquired their stake in 2021, after stepping in to help the carrier as it reeled from the pandemic-related travel disruptions and the 2019 bankruptcy of its UK parent company Thomas Cook.

The airline received state support totaling €930 million ($1.06 billion at the current exchange rate), which it fully paid off by March this year.

Skip next section Rhine levels near Koblenz on record low

Rhine levels near Koblenz on record low

Even with the summer officially over in Germany, the Rhine River, one of the country's essential trade routes, continues to dry up.

The latest data indicate that a gauge at Kaub, near the city of Koblenz, showed only 2 centimeters (less than an inch) of water on Thursday. This would make it the lowest value ever recorded since the measurement began in 1856.

By Friday, it had somewhat recovered to reach 5 centimeters.

It is important to note that these values show the water depth only at the gauge point, which is located relatively close to the shore. The actual navigable depth at Kaub is around 113 centimeters deeper than what's shown at the measuring point.

However, German shipping associations use the gauge value as a reference. Previously, the German Inland Waterways Association (BDB) stated that the Rhine is no longer fully navigable if the gauge values drop into single digits.

Any interruption of Rhine commercial traffic carries major economic risks for Germany. Many businesses use the river as a shipping lane connecting them to large North Sea harbors. In 2023, the Kiel Institute for the World Economy calculated that for every 30 days of low water on the Rhine, Germany's industrial production declines by about 1%.

Skip next section Saxony's interior minister questions Germany's asylum right

Saxony's interior minister questions Germany's asylum right

A four-point plan by conservative Saxon state Interior Minister Armin Schuster aims to limit the right to asylum by changing the European Convention on Human Rights and likely the German constitution, known as the Basic Law, according to multiple media reports.

The minister's plan, seen by the DPA news agency and Redaktionsnetzwerk Deutschland, says the German cities' and municipalities' ability to cope with asylum-seekers should determine how many are allowed in the country, rather than the current law that grants the right to asylum to anyone persecuted on political grounds.

Schuster's initiative would also see rejected asylum-seekers taken into custody in order to ensure deportation.

Germany's laws would be amended to allow a "deportation mandate."

"In order to fully implement the shift in migration policy, we need to ensure deportation for people who are ordered to leave, including criminals and those who do not integrate," Schuster said.

Skip next section Students to protest against potential return of military conscription

Students to protest against potential return of military conscription

Over 100 protests are expected across Germany as students push back on what they believe to be government's efforts to reintroduce military conscription.

The idea has been floated by senior politicians, including a former defense minister and the current premier of Bavaria earlier this month.

Germany has seen several waves of protests against the idea in recent years.

The immediate trigger for the school strike on Friday, however, is the military testing drive for young men in the northern state of Schleswig-Holstein. According to protest organizers, authorities are calling for men born in 2008 to be tested even if they have previously declared no interest in serving in the military.

A spokeswoman for the German Defense Ministry confirmed that the examination is mandatory regardless of the teenagers' stated preferences, though the policy has not yet been implemented all over the country.

Germany suspended mandatory military conscription in 2011.

Skip next section German parliament expected to approve fuel tax cut

German parliament expected to approve fuel tax cut

With oil prices still high on global markets, the German government is cutting the tax on gas and diesel at the gas station, with the move expected to pass the federal parliament later on Friday.

In order to save time, the government has attached the legal changes to a different law. If the measure is passed, it will save German drivers up to 16.7 euro cents per liter (about $0.72 per US gallon) from October 1.

The ADAC motoring association reported that average gas prices in Germany hit a record high last week, reaching €2.308 for a liter of super E10 unleaded and €2.471 for a liter of diesel ($9.98/US gallon and $10.69/US gallon, respectively).

Gas stations are not obligated to pass the full savings to the customers. However, a similar tax cut introduced earlier this year showed a strong effect on gas prices in May and June.

The measure is expected to stay in effect until the end of the year.

entries.title: Iranian President Pezeshkian brought a diplomatic tone to New York for UNGA. What did his remarks signal?
entries.summary: Iran's president used his trip to New York this week for the UN General Assembly to signal openness to talks over the nuclear dispute. However, the chances of a major breakthrough on the war remain low.
entries.content:
Iran

Amid Iran war, what did Pezeshkian achieve at UN?

September 25, 2026

Iran's president used his trip to New York this week for the UN General Assembly to signal openness to talks over the nuclear dispute. However, the chances of a major breakthrough on the war remain low.

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, who traveled to New York to attend the UN General Assembly this week, specifically made time to meet with American journalists and media representatives.

In an interview with the conservative US broadcaster Fox News, he signaled a willingness to make concessions in the nuclear dispute with the United States.

Washington has made clear that Iran must never be allowed to possess nuclear weapons. Asked whether Iran was prepared to hand over its highly enriched uranium, Pezeshkian said his country would comply with its obligations under international law and the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty.

In its most recent assessment, the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) estimated that Iran had more than 440 kilograms of uranium enriched to up to 60%.

Since the US-Israeli attacks on Iranian nuclear facilities in 2025, Iran has suspended its cooperation with the IAEA. The agency has continued to demand access to Iranian facilities and updated information on its nuclear stockpile and the whereabouts of its nuclear material.

Asked point-blank "Do you want a nuclear bomb or not?" during the exclusive interview on Fox News' "Special Report," Pezeshkian firmly rejected the premise.

"Not at all. Not at all. Our martyred, esteemed supreme leader had announced several times that, from a religious decree, it is unholy. It is illegal," he told host Bret Baier, referencing religious edicts issued against weapons of mass destruction.

Despite Pezeshkian's claims, the IAEA has assessed that Iran's fissile material is being enriched far beyond what is needed for civilian use.

Diplomacy: A first step?

A major breakthrough in the conflict between Iran and the United States is not expected anytime soon, Iran expert Arman Mahmoudian, a lecturer in Middle East Studies at the University of South Florida, told DW.

"Pezeshkian does not have the authority to initiate comprehensive de-escalation with the United States. In particular, hard-liners and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps appear to continue to wield considerable influence over Iran's decision-making process," he added.

Nevertheless, Mahmoudian thinks Pezeshkian's visit could help establish a more direct channel of communication between Tehran and Washington.

He also sees the possibility of creating a framework for future negotiations in New York, adding that the two sides could develop a road map that would pave the way for more substantive talks and, in the longer term, potentially contribute to de-escalation.

There are already signs of this, including meetings between Iranian and US delegations earlier this week. The White House, meanwhile, has confirmed that "positive and constructive" talks were continuing through intermediaries.

Hormuz — and Houthis — as leverage

The future of the Strait of Hormuz is also at the center of the discussions. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi reportedly said that Tehran had presented Washington with a proposal to resume negotiations.

Under the proposal, the strategically important waterway could be reopened within seven days if certain conditions were met. It remains unclear what those conditions are.

In the past, Iran has demanded the release of frozen Iranian assets, an end to the US blockade of Iranian ports and vessels, and a commitment by Washington not to interfere in Iran's internal affairs.

The Strait of Hormuz, through which around 20 million barrels of oil normally pass every day — roughly 20% of global oil consumption — has become one of Iran's most important sources of leverage.

The United States has failed to eliminate all of Iran's capabilities to threaten shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, Kelly Grieco, a senior fellow at the Stimson Center, told DW in July.

This is despite the US attacks having caused significant damage to Iran's navy and defense industry.

"At a certain point, it becomes really hard to find some of these targets," said Grieco. "They're mobile. They're distributed."

Without a long-term strategy, Grieco warned, the United States could therefore become trapped in a recurring cycle: Iran rebuilds its military capabilities, Washington launches another round of attacks and the cycle repeats itself.

Nearly seven months after the start of the Iran war, the conflict has also spread to a second strategically important shipping route.

The Iran-backed Houthi movement has expanded its control over Yemen's Red Sea coast and the strategically important area around the Bab al-Mandab Strait. This gives Iran another important lever along major international shipping routes.

Balancing pressure and negotiations

Middle East expert Mahmoudian expects Iran to continue pursuing a dual strategy of military pressure and diplomacy, saying that Tehran is likely to continue using the Strait of Hormuz as leverage and to prevent a full return to normal shipping traffic.

"At the same time, Iran will most likely continue rebuilding its military and strategic infrastructure inside the country," he said. "Reports suggest that Iranian authorities are already moving quickly to reconstruct some damaged facilities."

On the diplomatic front, he added that Iran is likely to continue negotiations with the US, either directly or through intermediaries.

Tehran is aware that the current situation, with the continuing threat of military attacks, sanctions and economic pressure, is not sustainable in the long term, Mahmoudian said, adding that Iran will therefore continue to have an interest in reaching a political agreement with Washington.

A deal with Iran will require time and difficult negotiations, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in New York on September 23, playing down expectations of a quick agreement. At the same time, he stressed that President Donald Trump has military options at his disposal alongside the diplomatic route.

This article was originally written in German.

entries.title: Pakistan's Sharif rails against India, praises Trump at UNGA
entries.summary: Pakistan's prime minister blamed India for last year's clashes, and credited the US president with preventing "all-out war" between two nuclear powers. Albania's PM told the UN delegates an anecdote about AI misuse.
entries.content:
Published September 22, 2026last updated September 26, 2026

Pakistan's prime minister blamed India for last year's clashes, and credited the US president with preventing "all-out war" between two nuclear powers. Albania's PM told the UN delegates an anecdote about AI misuse.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Pakistan's prime minister called for renewed peace talks between the US and Iran
  • Shehbaz Sharif also took aim at India on a number of issues, from clashes in 2025 to Kashmir, the Indus River System, and allegations of Islamophobia
  • Lebanese PM Nawaf Salam called for peacekeepers to remain in his country as Israel operates in a self-declared 'security zone' in south Lebanon
  • Edi Rama told the chamber the tale of how AI was used to whip up false fears of a fabricated Israeli invasion of the Albanian coastline
  • St. Lucia urged the UN and its members not to forget Haiti amid larger conflicts around the world
  • Tuvalu called for Taiwan to be granted full UN membership

This blog is paused. Read below for all the top headlines, videos and analyses on the 81 UN General Assembly from September 22-28, 2026:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section We are pausing our coverage

We are pausing our coverage

As the fourth day of the 81st UN General Assembly comes to a halt, we are pausing this blog for the night.

Today was another address-packed day, with several small island nations stressing the urgent need to address climate change, as they are most vulnerable to its consequences.

Norway and Sweden stressed the importance of continuing to support the UN, including with funds, as well as making it more representative by giving Africa a permanent seat on the Security Council.

Meanwhile, Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif took aim at India, rehashing in his address a short-lived conflict between the two countries last year. Sharif said his country faced "external aggression from India under a false pretext," adding that his country's response was "its inherent right of self-defense."

Before the session wrapped, India used its right of reply to address Pakistan's "bizarre remarks," and accuse its neighbor of terrorism. Pakistan was quick to respond, accusing New Delhi of "export[ing] terrorism and violence."

We will be back again tomorrow, when addresses from India, Germany, Russia, China, Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Canada, and others are scheduled.

Skip next section Day 4 at UNGA: Egypt, Norway, Sweden, Mexico outline priorities during afternoon session

Day 4 at UNGA: Egypt, Norway, Sweden, Mexico outline priorities during afternoon session

Skip next section Small island states take aim at world leaders for inaction on climate change

Small island states take aim at world leaders for inaction on climate change

The speakers for the small island nations of St. Kitts and Nevis, Samoa and Tonga called to attention the inaction of world leaders on climate change.

The island nations are disproportionately vulnerable to the climate crisis, with the deputy prime minister of Samoa, Mulipola Anarosa Ale Molioo, calling climate change "the single greatest threat" facing the country and the world.

Molioo stressed the need to scale up climate financing because small islands should not bear the cost of challenges of the climate crisis they did little to create.

Fatafehi Fakafanua, Prime Minister of Tonga, said Pacific leaders have been warning about the climate crisis, with little support for years.

Fakafanua said the question was not whether the world has heard the message of climate change but rather, he asked, "why has it still not acted?"

The deputy prime minister of St. Kitts and Nevis, Geoffrey Hanley, outlined some of the solutions his country has undertaken, such as investing in desalination and improving food security.

Hanley said that small states, who stand most at risk from the consequences of climate change, were still delivering big solutions.

But he said, because no small island state can perpetually adapt to the climate crisis, "adaptation cannot excuse inaction elsewhere."

Skip next section Iran says it gave US 7-day plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz

Iran says it gave US 7-day plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz

Iran has given the US a seven-day plan that would involve reopening the critical Strait of Hormuz to maritime navigation, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Friday.

Speaking to reporters at the United Nations General Assembly on Friday, Araghchi said the plan was delivered via Qatar and the choice now rests with Washington to meet the conditions Tehran has laid out.

"Iran does not accept coercion, threats or intimidation, and Iran will not surrender its sovereign rights under pressure," he said.

Skip next section Sharif blames India for 2025 clashes, calls for 'just and fair' Kashmir resolution

Sharif blames India for 2025 clashes, calls for 'just and fair' Kashmir resolution

Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif also took aim at India in his speech as he discussed the limited military clashes between the uneasy neighbors last year. 

"A year ago, Pakistan faced external aggression from India under a false pretext," the prime minister alleged. "Pakistan exercised its inherent right of self-defense under Article 51 of the United Nations charter."

He praised the country's military saying, "They silenced the enemy, repulsed its attack, and taught it a lesson it shall never ever forget," as the UN's TV feed cut to an Indian observer in the assembly shaking his head as he listened.

Pakistan considers Indian missile strikes on May 7 to be the start of the low-level conflict, that ran for less than a week, while India contends that the strikes were retalliation for an attack in Indian-administered Jammu and Kashmir in late April. New Delhi had accused Pakistan of supporting cross-border terrorism, which Islambad denied.

Sharif praised US President Donald Trump's "resolute and visionary leadership," crediting it with saving "hundreds of millions of lives in South Asia" by intervening and helping to broker a truce "when two nuclear neighbors stood at the brink of all-out war."

Sharif asked "who knows the extent of devastation that could have taken place" without Trump's "clarity of thought and action" at a critical moment.

He said it was necessary to ensure that South Asia "never reaches this precipice again," and said that doing so would require "a just and fair resolution of the Kashmir dispute." 

He said Kashmiri people had been waiting eight decades for the UN to "fulfill its solemn commitment of a free and impartial plebiscite under its auspices." He also criticized recent "attempts to alter the legal status of Jammu and Kashmir through demographic reengineering and other illegal measures."

He also criticized India for its decision to hold a treat on the Indus River System in abeyance, saying this move had "no legal basis whatsoever." 

Skip next section Pakistan's Sharif: Hormuz, Bab el-Mandeb are 'arteries of global economy' and 'must remain open'

Pakistan's Sharif: Hormuz, Bab el-Mandeb are 'arteries of global economy' and 'must remain open'

Pakistan's Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif touted his country's efforts to mediate in the war between the US and Iran since February, particularly in reaching the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding that brought an uneasy calm to hostilities for a few weeks earlier this year — albeit without resolving many of the wider issues in the conflict.

"Regrettably, Mr. President, recently we have witnessed a dangerous surge of hostilties," Sharif said. "Yet amid the roar of missiles, drones and guns, the voice for diplomacy must echo even louder and stronger."

"The Strait of Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb are arteries of the global economy," Sharif said, also referring to the western entry to the Red Sea coming under increasing pressure from the Iran-aligned Houthis. "They must remain open, connecting nations, not becoming the chokepoints of confrontation." 

Sharif said these waters "must carry the promise of prosperity, not the perils of war."

He said Pakistan condemned recent "deplorable" Houthi attacks against Saudi Arabia "in the strongest possible terms," not least the reported attempted drone attack on the holy city of Mecca, which he said had "outraged Muslims across the globe."

Skip next section Albania's Rama tells of 'Flamingo Revolution,' warning not of a rogue AI, but one following rogue orders

Albania's Rama tells of 'Flamingo Revolution,' warning not of a rogue AI, but one following rogue orders

Prime Minister Edi Rama told the chamber that while Albania was not a developer of "frontier models" in AI, "we are a nation that has already lived the future others are still debating," given how outside actors had tried out the technology's darker capabilites on its citizens.

Rama said he felt he owed the chamber a "simple message," if not necessarily the one most commonly discussed during the week.

"The greatest immediate danger is not that artificial intelligence will stop obeying humanity. The greatest danger is that it will obey the wrong human beings perfectly," he said.

"The public debate imagines machines that awaken, acquire ambitions and turn against their creators," Rama said. "But the systems confronting us today do not wake up with hatred in their hearts, they multiply ours. They have no ambition of their own, they serve the ambition of others. They carry no flag, but they can be deployed by a state. They tell no lie for their own benefit, but they can tell a billion lies on others' behalf."

Rama mentioned how Albania had become the first government to launch an AI minister. He said this showed his government's belief that "inside an accountable state," the technology could be used to "reduced the distance between citizens and public services."

But he said Albania had also learned how "artificial intelligence outside accountability can be used to eliminate the distance between a lie and the human mind."

He relayed the story of the so-called "Flamingo Revolution," a "fabricated narrative of an Israeli invasion of the Albanian coast."

This entirely fictional invasion "was manufactured, was personalized and delivered through voices, pages and channels citizens already trusted." Rama explained how the details of the overarching story were personalized to maximize their impact with the individuals reading them.

"Different fabriactions entered different emotional worlds, all serving the same strategic lie," he said. "The consequences were real. Citizens had their own reasons to protest — don't take me wrong. But suddenly, they started to protest also against a phantom enemy. Antisemitic tropes entered our public discourse for the first time ever."

Rama said that amid the AI disinformation drive, "fear became anger, anger became mobilization and fabrication became political reality." 

"And this was not a laboratory experiment. I'm not talking to you about a science fiction movie. It was a Tuesday, in Tirana, our capital city."

Rama said it wasn't an algorithm that invented the objective, but rather a human actor. The algorithm didn't develop hatred, but "it discovered how to activate ours."

He called this particular use case "systematic fraud as a service," and warned its potential for use in scenarios like elections were just as real as in trying to amplify animosity to war in the Middle East.

Skip next section St. Lucia urges assembly not to forget Haiti in war-torn world

St. Lucia urges assembly not to forget Haiti in war-torn world

Prime Minister Philip Pierre from the Caribbean island of Saint Lucia said his country "laments the continued conflicts and human suffering across the globe," listing some of the most notable wars in Ukraine, Gaza, the wider Middle East and Sudan. 

He said his country of around 184,000 people called for the establishment of a Palestinian state with full UN membership.

Pierre then turned to a Caribbean conflict that has featured rather less this week in New York, Haiti. 

"Member states of this organization must act in a manner that will restore the trust of the people of Haiti in the United Nations," Pierre said. "Some member states have failed to meet the commitments and pledges to the gang suppression force in Haiti, whose one-year mandate ends this month." 

He urged the Security Council to renew the force's mandate, and called on member states to provide it with sufficient "resources to operation effectively and successfully."

He said that while gang violence was "the main factor to be resolved," the crisis in the country was "multidimensional." 

"The international response must include long-term socio-economic assistance that will help restore an acceptable quality of life for the people of Haiti," he said.

Skip next section Pacific archipelago Tuvalu appeals for climate finance, Taiwanese UN membership

Pacific archipelago Tuvalu appeals for climate finance, Taiwanese UN membership

Tuvalu's Prime Minister Hristijan Mickoski told the assembly that climate change "is and remains the single, greatest existential threat to Tuvalu's survival, security and sustainable development."

He said the low-lying archipelago of some 10,000 people acknowledged global efforts to contain the climate crisis but said the "pace and scale of global actions remain insufficient."

Mickoscki called for a "fast, fair, just and orderly transition away from fossil fuels."

He called for moves to provide climate financing "as grants" to allow countries like his to better prepare and adapt for coming changes.

He said his country was keenly anticipating the pre-COP meetings this October, prior to the main UN COP31 summit in Turkey in November.

"Tuvalu may have only 26 square kilometers of land," he said, "but we are custodians of some 750,000 square kilometers of ocean, which makes Tuvalu a large ocean state."

Tuvalu joins Palau in appealing for Taiwanese membership

Tuvalu is also known as one of just 12 countries in the world to retain full diplomatic relations with Taiwan, rather than having formal ties to China. 

Mickoscki said that the UN "must also uphold the principles of dignity, inclusion and equality" for everyone.

"Yet, too many communities remain outside the structures designed to serve all humanity," he said. "Tuvalu therefore calls for arrangements that enable the meaningful participation of the 23.3 million people of Taiwan in the United Nations and its specialized agencies and mechanisms."

He said that Taipei had consistently demonstrated that it was an "able, trustworthy and constructive partner," saying its UN exclusion "undermines both the spirit and effectiveness of multilateral cooperation."

The People's Republic of China took over the Chinese seat at the UN — and the Security Council veto that came with it — in 1971, more than two decades after the Chinese Communist revolution. Since then, Taiwan has been excluded from the UN for more than half a century since then, with no clear route towards membership, given that it is only possible with Beijing's blessing.

Not far away, during his state visit to Washington DC to speak with President Donald Trump, China's Xi Jinping on Thursday appealed to Trump to change the US stance on Taiwanese independence from not "supporting" it to openly "opposing" it. 

Skip next section Lebanese prime minister says 'the problem is not the absence of rules'

Lebanese prime minister says 'the problem is not the absence of rules'

Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam told the UN that "without mutual trust, peace and security cannot take root among states, nor can competition among them flourish."

He said that the UN was founded, more than 80 years ago, on "the promise that the force of law would replace the law of force."

But Salam said that wars and conflicts still plague a world that spends more on armaments than on development.

"The problem is not the absence of rules," Salam said. "It is their selective application, if not their outright non-application."

He did not mention Israel by name in his preamble but did later in his speech. 

Salam said his government had three commitments to fulfil, and argued that all three were interconnected:

  • Restoring trust and credibility in Lebanese authorities after the economic collapse and vast port explosion in Beirut of August 4, 2020
  • Ensuring that only the Lebanese government held weapons and made decisions of war for the country — comments seemingly aimed at the pro-Iranian Hezbollah group, which he did not name 
  • Reclaiming occupied Lebanese territory from Israel under the terms of UN Resolution 1701 adopted to end the Second Lebanon War between Israel and Hezbollah in 2006

"Our position on the war has been clear from the outset," Salam said. "We want it to end. We want the ceasefire consolidated. We want Israel to withdraw from all Lebanese territory up to our internationally recognized borders, in accordance with the 1949 General Armistice Agreement and as affirmed by Resolution 1701. We want the release of all our detainees, the safe and dignified return of our people to their villages and towns, and a reconstruction of what the war destroyed."

Under the tense ceasefire deal between Lebanon and Israel, brokered by the US, Israel is supposed to withdraw its forces from a self-declared "buffer zone" in southern Lebanon. In turn, Lebanon's government is supposed to move its military fores into these areas and stop Hezbollah from using them to launch attacks into northern Israel. The current goal is to create so-called pilot zones where the Lebanese army moves in and Israel's troops move out. 

The process is making only gradual progress, as both sides accuse the other of failing to meet their obligations.

Skip next section Lebanon PM calls for peacekeeping troops after UNIFIL mandate ends

Lebanon PM calls for peacekeeping troops after UNIFIL mandate ends

Lebanon Prime Minister Nawaf Salam has called for the UN to keep its UNIFIL (UN Interim Force in Lebanon) peacekeeping troops in place after their mandate expires at year's end.

"What we wish to stress here and today is the need to avert the vacuum that UNIFIL's withdrawal could create, were it to take place without agreement on a new international force to replace it," he said.

The UN's troops, currently numbering 7,500 from 46 different countries, have been in Lebanon since 1978.

Last year, however, the US pushed the UN Security Council to terminate the mandate when it ran out.

UNIFIL's expected departure comes as Israel maintains troops in its own self-declared "security zone" extending some 10 kilometers (6 miles) into south Lebanon.

Skip next section Welcome back to our coverage

Welcome back to our coverage

We are resuming our coverage of the United Nations General Assembly on Friday, September 25.

The general debate is scheduled to begin its fourth day of the assembly at 9 a.m. New York time (1300 UTC).

Iraq, Pakistan, Lebanon and others are to speak in today's morning session, while countries such as Egypt, Mexico, Kazakhstan and Sweden will take the stand in the afternoon.

Friday's debate comes after a day of speeches that was centered on Gaza, with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's address sparking a walkout by several delegates.

Skip next section That's a wrap on Day 3 of UNGA

That's a wrap on Day 3 of UNGA

We're wrapping up for the day, with the third day's sessions of the 81st General Assembly now complete.

Gaza dominated the speeches today.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu addressed the assembly, denying that his country's actions in Gaza amount to genocide, an accusation leveled by several speakers on Thursday, including Palestinian Prime Minister Mahmoud Abbas.

Several delegates exited the hall as the Israeli prime minister began his speech.

Protesters had also gathered outside the UN Headquarters in New York ahead of Netanyahu's address, with some being arrested.

Before the session wrapped up, the representatives of Iran, Turkey and Qatar used their right of reply to lambast Netanyahu's address.

Join us on Friday, when Iraq, Lebanon, Pakistan, Egypt, Mexico, Haiti, Norway, Sweden and others are due to address the assembly.

Skip next section Nepal's leader says his country is paying the price of climate change

Nepal's leader says his country is paying the price of climate change

Four weeks after catastrophic flash floods ravaged Nepal, the small Himalayan country's young prime minister stood at the podium of the UN General Assembly to warn leaders about the impact of a warming world.

"I wish I could stand here today simply to speak about development, democracy, peace and the hopes of a young nation. Instead, I must speak about death and destruction of epic proportions," said Balendra Shah as he began his address to the UNGA on Thursday.

Nepal's leader calls for international cooperation for protecting the Himalayas

The Nepalese leader stressed that the perils of climate change transcend national borders as he made a case for greater international cooperation for protecting the Himalayas.

"The Himalayas are not peripheral to the planet. They are part of the planet's life-support system," Shah said, proposing the establishment of a "Himalayan Climate Resilience Mechanism," which he said would be led by Nepal, India and China.

Shah elaborated that the mechanism would help countries share satellite data and expertise, as well as monitor glacial lakes that pose a threat. He also called for stronger joint early-warning systems and coordinated, cross-border assistance in the event of a disaster. 

"Let the Himalayas become a laboratory of international cooperation, rather than a frontier of fragmented information," the prime minister said.

Nepal's leader says his country is paying the price of climate change

Shah noted that his country only contributes less than 0.1% of global greenhouse gas emissions.

"We did not create this crisis. Yet we are paying a colossal price for it," he said, adding that he wasn not blaming any nation or continent.

"We are not here to turn climate change into another geopolitical battlefield. We are here to ask everyone to recommit to shared responsibility and solidarity," Shah said.

Nepal seeks grants, not loans, for flood recovery

The Nepalese prime minister emphasized the principles of "Responsibility, Reparation and Resilience" as he called for grant-based support rather than loans.

Shah said that vulnerable nations should not be forced to take on additional debt to recover from climate catastrophes.

"When a climate-driven disaster destroys the infrastructure of a poor country, the answer cannot simply be another mega loan or a patchwork of small grants. We need adequate grant-based support from the world," he said.

36-year-old Shah was theyoungest head of government to speak at the 81st session of the UNGA.

Skip next section 'Hands off ICC,' Dutch PM says amid growing US pressure

'Hands off ICC,' Dutch PM says amid growing US pressure

Netherlands Prime Minister Rob Jetten, addressing the General Assembly on Thursday, said the International Criminal Court, which is based in The Hague, was "under attack."

Jetten did not name the US or President Donald Trump, who on Tuesday urged countries to leave the court, the latest move in his administration's campaign against the ICC.

"How can you possibly be opposed to prosecuting the very worst crimes?" Jetten asked the assembly, drawing loud applause from the delegates.

"I believe there can be only one response. To say: hands off the ICC, and all those other institutions that protect the international legal order. Because the reality is that we still need to fight impunity."

Washington has imposed financial sanctions and visa bans on ICC staff, with officials reportedly preparing additional sanctions that could curtail the court's ability to operate.

entries.title: DW shows solidarity with Georgians' commitment to democracy
entries.summary: Cultural and media professionals in Georgia remain under threat. A DW panel brings together insiders who share their hopes and fears.
entries.content:
September 25, 2026

Cultural and media professionals in Georgia remain under threat. A DW panel brings together insiders who share their hopes and fears.

"I personally don't feel safe as a citizen in my country and as a person who has worked for independent media for a long time," Georgian media expert and advocate for press freedom Nino Robakidze told DW. Her activism with international civil society groups has made her a target in her home country.

Similarly, Georgian journalists are currently facing "physical threats, digital threats, psychological threats. And there is also financial and legal pressure around their media organizations," she reported.

Robakidze was one of the participants at DW's panel discussion "Democracy under pressure? The situation for cultural and media professionals in Georgia," held on Thursday in Berlin's James-Simon-Galerie.

Host Jochen Rosenkranz, director of DW's Culture and Sports department, pointed out in his introduction that it had been difficult to find Georgians willing to participate in the panel. Many had refused, saying they feared the repercussions not only for themselves, but also for their friends and family.

"We're all afraid of the intimidation," Georgian-born musician, filmmaker, journalist and cultural organizer Marika Lapauri-Burk explained. She nevertheless agreed to take part in the discussion, alongside Nino Robakidze and journalist Juri Rescheto, head of DW's Riga bureau.

Lapauri-Burk added that the government had become increasingly creative in its arbitrary reasons to detain those with critical voices.

Local civil society groups and human rights organizations estimate that from 90 to over 100 political dissidents and protesters are currently imprisoned or in pre-trial detention.

Russian influence impacting democratization efforts

Once thought of as a leading democracy of the Caucasus region, Georgia is undergoing a rapid transition toward authoritarianism under the Georgian Dream (GD) party, in power now since 2012.

The party originally declared itself pro-European, but in recent years has sought more overtly to align with Russia. The party gained an increased majority in a contested October 2024 parliamentary election.

A month later, the GD announced the suspension of EU accession negotiations until 2028, despite a substantial majority of Georgians strongly favoring European integration. Halting the talks ignited demonstrations across the country as the government increasingly aligned its policies with Moscow. 

But the transformation could be felt years before the election: "The real pressure on independent media and professional journalists escalated after Russia's unprovoked invasion in Ukraine," says Robakidze. An important anti-Western campaign followed the invasion, which "had a huge impact on Georgian media environment at large," she added.

The country was also rocked by anti-government protests in 2023-2024 as pro-EU protesters took to the streets. They were  pushing back against new, Russian-style "foreign agents" legislation, which required all organizations that received foreign funding to register with the state and comply with extensive reporting requirements.

That came into force in June 2025, and a stricter version has introduced criminal liability and prison sentences of up to five years for individuals and groups who fail to register their activities as being "under foreign influence."

Culture directly affected by the law

Many independent cultural institutions, festivals, arts organizations and heritage projects are heavily reliant on funding from the European Union, European foundations and international cultural programs.

Critics say the law stigmatizes institutions for their vaguely defined "foreign influence."

The same laws that target activists and journalists threaten the grants, partnerships and institutions that have connected Georgian artists to Europe for decades.

The state agency responsible for enforcing the "foreign agents" law, known as the Anti-Corruption Bureau, uses the law to persecute prominent civil society groups, launching inspections and freezing their bank accounts.

Another law also operates in tandem with the controversial "foreign agent" legislation.

Georgia's anti-LGBTQ law, officially a legislative package entitled "On Family Values and the Protection of Minors," explicitly bans the "popularization" or "propaganda" of same-sex relationships and non-binary gender identities in public spaces, media, education and the arts.

Freedom of expression under threat

Cultural producers are forced to risk choosing between self-censorship, shutting down entirely or facing severe state retaliation.

"The situation is becoming increasingly difficult for critical thinkers — especially artists," explained Juri Rescheto, who notes that many critical thinkers can be found within artistic circles. They are affected "not only in their art but also in their private lives," he added.

Rescheto cited the example of a small gallery he visited in the city of Gori, where protesters' slogans were projected onto a wall as part of an exhibition. It all felt "harmless, really — or so we would say here in the West," the journalist said. Yet the gallery is now facing closure because the city refuses to renew their lease since the action, he added.

Artists have generally been playing a powerful role in the protests: "There were many actions that were very artistically conceived," Lapauri-Burk noted.

"Ode to Joy" from Ludwig van Beethoven's 9th Symphony — the official anthem of the European Union — has often been played as a pro-European symbol of democratic resistance at anti-government protests in Tbilisi, Georgia, Rescheto added.

DW's new Georgian-language service

This year, Georgia is the focus of the Beethovenfest's Campus Project; a cultural exchange project developed in cooperation with DW. 

"Music transcends borders and language barriers and brings people together," DW's director general Barbara Massing noted at the opening of the panel discussion, which also celebrated the recent launch of DW's new Georgian-language service on Instagram. Georgian has now become Deutsche Welle's 33rd language.

"With the new Georgian-language service in cooperation with France Medias Monde and TVP World, we are strengthening the European commitment to free media and trustworthy information in a region that is specifically targeted by disinformation campaigns and faces unique political and social challenges," said Massing.

Robakidze welcomes such an initiation supporting Georgians who still hope for a democratic future. Severe fatigue, state crackdowns and a sense of despair among participants is seeing protest dwindling. Even so, "We still need to remain ready to take action," she said. To that end, "We need all the media support we can get."

Edited by: Hans Kellett

entries.title: Xi wraps up US visit with trip to National Archives
entries.summary: On the last day of his visit to the US, Chinese leader Xi Jinping visited the National Archives with President Donald Trump. The Archives store the Declaration of Independence and the US Constitution.
entries.content:
United States of America

Xi wraps up US visit with trip to National Archives

Published September 24, 2026last updated September 25, 2026

On the last day of his visit to the US, Chinese leader Xi Jinping visited the National Archives with President Donald Trump. The Archives store the Declaration of Independence and the US Constitution.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • On the last day of Xi Jinping's visit, he and Donald Trump, along with their spouses, had tea at the White House.
  • Trump praised the progress he and Xi had made during Xi's visit to the US.
  • Xi said he expected two more meetings with Trump this year.
  • Trump and Xi visited the National Archives after the tea session.
  • On Thursday, following the talks, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping and their wives attended a state dinner hosted in honor of the Chinese leader.

This blog is now closed.

Follow along here for updates on Xi's state visit to the US:

Skip next section Thank you for reading!

Thank you for reading!

With Chinese leader Xi Jinping on his way back home, we are ending our coverage of his three-day visit to the US.

This was the second summit between Xi and US President Donald Trump this year, as well as the Chinese leader's first visit to Washington in over a decade.

Although both leaders made optimistic statements during the summit, no breakthrough was achieved.

Skip next section Trump confirms 2 more meetings with Xi this year

Trump confirms 2 more meetings with Xi this year

After Chinese leader Xi Jinping left Washington, President Donald Trump announced that he will meet with him again in November in China and in December at the G20 summit in Florida.

"The meeting was one of Friendship, Strength, and Success, for both China and the USA," Trump wrote about his summit with Xi on his Truth Social platform.

"Much has been, and will be, accomplished. I look forward to our next meeting!" he added.

Skip next section Xi leaves US for Beijing

Xi leaves US for Beijing

According to the Xinhua news agency, Chinese leader Xi Jinping left Washington, concluding his three-day visit to the US.

CNN reported that Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, had a red carpet departure at Joint Base Andrews after visiting the National Archives with President Donald Trump and First Lady Melania Trump.

Skip next section Xi and Trump examine sacred texts of US democracy at National Archives

Xi and Trump examine sacred texts of US democracy at National Archives

Skip next section Trump confirms he discussed Iran war with Xi

Trump confirms he discussed Iran war with Xi

US President Donald Trump said he discussed the Iran war with his visiting Chinese counterpart, Xi Jinping.

When asked if they had discussed Iran, Trump replied, "We did," as he showed Xi around the National Archives in Washington.

Trump was also asked if he thought there would be progress on reopening the Strait of Hormuz. He replied, "I think we're going to do great."

Skip next section Xi says he expects to meet with Trump 2 more times this year

Xi says he expects to meet with Trump 2 more times this year

Meanwhile, Chinese President Xi Jinping suggested the possibility of two more meetings with US President Donald Trump this year.

"Looking ahead to the remainder of this year, there will be two more opportunities for us to meet each other — firstly the APEC meeting in China and then the G20 summit in the United States," Xi said through a translator at the White House.

"I do welcome you, Mr President and the First Lady, to visit China," he added.

Trump responded, “We will, and we’ll be speaking a lot.”

Xi also said that the US-China relationship will be one of strategic stability based on respect, fairness, and reciprocity. He went on to say that he and Trump had agreed to add new substance to this relationship.

Skip next section Trump says he and Xi made 'tremendous strides'

Trump says he and Xi made 'tremendous strides'

President Donald Trump praised the progress he and Chinese leader Xi  Jinping had made during Xi's visit to the US.

"I think we've made tremendous strides, we've made great strides, very positive for both countries," Trump told journalists while he and his wife, Melania, were having tea with Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, at the White House.

Trump also added that the two sides will "be speaking a lot."

Skip next section US to reveal details on China trade talks on Monday

US to reveal details on China trade talks on Monday

The United States is expected to release details on the outcome of trade negotiations with China on Monday, according to US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer.

"We're in a managed trade situation ... ​we've had progress, and we will release on Monday, I think, a lot ​more details about what we've accomplished over the past ​few weeks ‌in negotiating with the Chinese," he told CNBC on Friday.

Greer also said that the US has agreed with China to exempt some key goods from trade disputes.

He added that the US would export agricultural products and medical devices, and import consumer goods and other "non-sensitive" items from China.

Greer also mentioned that the current talks did not cover a small amount of high-quality, US-made chips that require licenses.

Last April, the US increased import tariffs on Chinese goods in several stages, raising them to up to 145%. In response, China imposed counter-tariffs of up to 125% and restricted exports of certain materials.

The two sides later agreed to several 90-day suspensions of new tariffs before Trump and Xi reached a broader trade agreement in South Korea last October. The deal was set to expire in November.

Skip next section Xi wraps up US visit with tea and trip to National Archives

Xi wraps up US visit with tea and trip to National Archives

On the final day of Chinese President Xi Jinping's visit to the US, he and President Donald Trump, along with their spouses, are back at the White House for a tea session.

Then, the two leaders are scheduled to visit the National Archives, where the Declaration of Independence, the Constitution, and the Bill of Rights are kept.

After the tour, Xi is expected to leave Washington.

On Thursday, Trump and Xi met for talks at the White House, followed by a state dinner later in the day.

However, DW's analysis shows that little progress was made at the summit on key issues of US-Chinese relations, such as trade tensions and AI regulation. 

Skip next section What you need to know about Xi's meeting with Trump in Washington so far

What you need to know about Xi's meeting with Trump in Washington so far

US President Donald Trump on Thursday rolled out the red carpet for China's Xi Jinping on the Chinese president's first state visit to Washington in over a decade.

Ahead of the meeting, Xi said the US and China "should be partners rather than rivals," while Trump hailed his "truly great friendship" with the Chinese president. However, no breakthrough was expected in the trade tensions between the world's two largest economies.

The talks centered on the Middle East, Ukraine and the Korean Peninsula, according to a statement by Beijing. The US has not provided details about the meeting.

After the talks, Xi attended a lavish state dinner with Trump and US tech executives, including Meta's Mark Zuckerberg, OpenAI's Sam Altman, Amazon's Jeff Bezos and Tesla's Elon Musk.

Trump described the event as the "hottest ticket in town" and said the "entire tech world" and "entire banking world and a lot more" would attend.

On Friday, Xi is scheduled to visit the National Archives, where the US Declaration of Independence, Constitution and Bill of Rights are held.

Skip next section Protesters gather in downtown Washington to protest Xi's visit

Protesters gather in downtown Washington to protest Xi's visit

A few hundred protesters gathered near the White House to rally against Xi Jinping's visit to the US.

Protesters highlighted a number of issues, from calls for religious freedom and autonomy in Tibet, Hong Kong and the Xinjiang region to demands that China refrain from interfering in Taiwan.

Protesters gathered in Lafayette Park, north of the White House, while other groups gathered outside the Chinese embassy. Pro-Xi rallies were also held in Washington.

Skip next section Trump says he and Xi have 'never gotten along better' at dinner toast

Trump says he and Xi have 'never gotten along better' at dinner toast

US President Donald Trump continued to heap praise on his guest, Chinese President Xi Jinping, during a White House state dinner on Thursday.

"President Xi and I both understand we represent different systems, but the ties between our people endure, and we've never gotten along better," Trump said during his toast, adding that "together, we can continue to build a relationship that promotes prosperity and security for future generations."

Xi noted in his own toast that "President Trump has pledged to make America great again" and that "China is committed to achieving great national rejuvenation."

"These two goals are both ambitious and can surely be mutually reinforcing," Xi said.

Earlier discussions between Xi and Trump touched on tensions over Taiwan, trade and artificial intelligence.

Skip next section State dinner includes tech-heavy guest list, but Chinese CEOs are missing

State dinner includes tech-heavy guest list, but Chinese CEOs are missing
